alignment.note: The Vulgate transmits an entirely different verse (Mark 9:42, concerning causing little ones to stumble), while the Greek and Peshitta attest Mark 9:41 (the cup of water saying). This represents a verse-level textual displacement in the Vulgate manuscript tradition, likely due to scribal error or variant chapter division.

Greek employs the indefinite relative construction ὃς γὰρ ἄν ('whoever'), using three particles to express conditionality and generality. Syriac achieves the same semantic force with ܟܠ ܕܝܢ ('everyone who'), a simpler two-word construction typical of Semitic syntax.

Greek ποτίσῃ ὑμᾶς separates the verb from its object with accusative ὑμᾶς ('you'), while Syriac ܕܢܫܩܝܟܘܢ incorporates the pronominal suffix directly onto the verb ('gives-you-to-drink'), reflecting standard Syriac verb morphology versus Greek analytic structure.

The Peshitta inserts ܒܠܚܘܕ ('only, alone'), emphasizing the minimal nature of the gift (merely a cup of water). Neither the Greek NA28 nor any major Greek manuscript tradition attests this qualifier, suggesting a Syriac interpretive expansion for rhetorical emphasis.

Greek uses the prepositional phrase ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι μου ('in the name of me') with article and dative case. Syriac ܒܫܡܐ ('in [the] name') employs the emphatic state without separate article, as Syriac encodes definiteness morphologically rather than with free-standing articles.

Greek places the causal clause ὅτι Χριστοῦ ἐστε ('because you are of Christ') after 'in my name,' while Syriac ܕܕܡܫܝܚܐ ܐܢܬܘܢ ('that of-the-Messiah you-are') follows immediately. Both traditions express identical semantics but differ in clause sequencing, likely reflecting underlying Semitic versus Greek rhetorical preferences.

Greek ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν uses dative ὑμῖν as indirect object, while Syriac ܐܡܝܢ ܐܡܪ ܐܢܐ ܠܟܘܢ inserts the independent pronoun ܐܢܐ ('I') for emphasis and employs the prepositional phrase ܠܟܘܢ ('to you'). Syriac regularly makes subject pronouns explicit where Greek relies on verbal inflection alone.

Greek employs the emphatic double negative οὐ μὴ ἀπολέσῃ ('certainly not may lose'), a construction unique to Koine Greek for strong negation. Syriac ܕܠܐ ܢܘܒܕ ('that not he-will-lose') uses the simple negative particle ܕܠܐ with imperfect verb, achieving equivalent semantic force through different syntactic means.

Greek τὸν μισθὸν αὐτοῦ uses the article τόν with separate possessive pronoun αὐτοῦ ('the reward of-him'), while Syriac ܐܓܪܗ attaches the pronominal suffix directly to the noun ('his-reward'). This reflects the standard typological difference between Greek analytic and Syriac synthetic possessive constructions.
